items.text: High lung cancer risk does not equate to large net screening benefit; jointly quantifying competing mortality, treatment applicability, and procedural harms has practical scientific value.

Real-world screening cohorts from three systems can generate independent empirical knowledge on stratified complications, function, and lung function distributions, complementing healthier trial populations.

Linking cohort parameters with established microsimulation allows comparison of strategies and preference-sensitive thresholds; it can provide conditional decision insights without requiring a new RCT to be valuable.
Selection of screenees, survival/repeated screening, and confounding limit generalizability to all eligible individuals; early diagnosis is not direct proof of observational mortality benefit.

Functional proxies, indication-driven lung function measurements, and site missingness can misclassify key strata; multiple imputation/IPW cannot automatically resolve non-random missingness and measurement bias.

Simulated counterfactual survival and other mortality parameters require clear transportability, calibration/validation, and uncertainty; current guidelines, non-surgical treatments, and threshold preferences also affect net benefit interpretation.
